title: Two Kings and a Battle at the Pool of Gibeon
summary: Guided by the LORD, David moves to Hebron, where the men of Judah anoint him king, and he thanks the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul. Meanwhile Abner, Saul's commander, makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king over the rest of Israel. The two sides meet at the pool of Gibeon, where a contest between champions turns into a battle; David's men win, but Abner kills Joab's brother Asahel, and the seeds of a blood feud are sown.
story: Saul is dead, and David, who had waited years without seizing the throne, now asks the LORD where to go. The answer is Hebron, the old city of Abraham and the chief town of Judah, and there his own tribe anoints him king. That is only half the kingdom. The northern tribes, led by Saul's powerful commander Abner, rally around Saul's surviving son. For the first time Israel has two kings, and the chapter opens a civil war that will run through the next two chapters. David acts as a king of the whole people from the start, reaching out to Jabesh-gilead, a northern town loyal to Saul. But the chapter ends with a death that turns political struggle into personal vengeance, and Asahel's blood will shape what happens to Abner in chapter 3.
historical:
The events follow shortly after Saul's death, around 1010 BC. Hebron lies in the hill country of Judah about 19 miles (30 kilometers) south of Jerusalem, and it had strong associations with the patriarchs, who were buried nearby (Genesis 23, 49:29-32), and with Caleb's clan. David's marriage to Abigail, widow of a Calebite, and his gifts to the towns of Judah (1 Samuel 30:26-31) had prepared the ground. Abner takes Ish-bosheth to Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, out of reach of the Philistines who now controlled the valleys west of the river. The territories listed as Ish-bosheth's kingdom (Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin) describe a claim to the north more than firm control; the name read as Asher is uncertain in the Hebrew, and some take it as a different group.

The chronology is a known puzzle: Ish-bosheth reigns two years, but David is king at Hebron seven and a half. Common explanations are that Abner needed time to establish Ish-bosheth after the Philistine victory, or that David remained at Hebron for several years after the north joined him before taking Jerusalem. Gibeon, where the armies meet, is identified with el-Jib, north of Jerusalem, where excavations led by James Pritchard in the 1950s uncovered a large rock-cut pool and jar handles inscribed with the city's name; whether that pool is the one in this story cannot be proven.
cultural:
Anointing with oil was the sign that a person had been set apart for office. David had been anointed privately by Samuel years before (1 Samuel 16:13); now he is anointed publicly by the men of Judah, and later he will be anointed by the elders of all Israel (5:3). Kingship in Israel involved both God's choice and the people's recognition. Burying the dead honorably was a sacred duty, and David's message to Jabesh praises their chesed, their loyal kindness, toward Saul.

The name Ish-bosheth means man of shame. First Chronicles 8:33 gives Saul's son the name Eshbaal, man of Baal, and most scholars think the scribes who transmitted Samuel replaced baal (which could mean lord and was once used of the LORD) with bosheth, shame, once the word had become fixed as the name of a Canaanite god. The contest at Gibeon, twelve young men from each side, resembles representative combat, in which champions fought to settle a dispute without full battle; here it ends with all of them dead and solves nothing. The place name Helkath-hazzurim is usually taken to mean field of blades or field of flints, commemorating the slaughter. The ram's horn, the shofar, was blown to signal troops in battle.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts: David made king in Judah (verses 1-11) and the battle at Gibeon (12-32). The first half is calm and orderly, with David inquiring of the LORD and acting on the answer. The second is violent and chaotic, driven by commanders rather than kings: Abner and Joab make the decisions, and neither Ish-bosheth nor David appears. The Asahel episode is told slowly and with great care. Abner twice warns him to turn aside, and the narrator repeats the phrase about turning to the right or to the left. Asahel, fast as a gazelle, will not turn, and he dies. The line “every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen” lets the reader feel the weight of the death. Abner's plea at sunset, “Must the sword devour forever?”, names the tragedy of the whole conflict: these are brothers pursuing brothers.

outline.t: David anointed king of Judah; his message to Jabesh-gilead
Abner makes Ish-bosheth king of Israel
The contest and battle at the pool of Gibeon
The pursuit, the truce, and the reckoning

doctrines.note: David asks the LORD whether to go up and where, and he goes where he is told. The kingdom he has been promised does not arrive all at once, but God leads him step by step. The chapter shows faithful waiting continuing even after the obstacle of Saul is gone.

David's praise of Jabesh for their loyal kindness (chesed) and faithfulness (emet) uses the core vocabulary of covenant. He blesses them in the LORD's name and promises to show them the same favor, inviting even Saul's loyal supporters into a relationship of trust with the new king.

The needless deaths at Gibeon and the killing of Asahel show how quickly rivalry among God's people becomes bloodshed. Abner's question about the sword devouring forever names the self-perpetuating nature of violence once it starts.

words.note: Chesed, kindness, loyal love, or steadfast love. It is the love that keeps faith within a relationship, especially a covenant, and it is one of the great words of the Old Testament for God's own character. David praises the chesed Jabesh showed Saul and prays that the LORD will show them chesed in return. The word will return when David seeks to show chesed to Saul's family in chapter 9.

Emet, truth or faithfulness, often paired with chesed to describe love that is both warm and reliable. The pair describes the LORD himself in Exodus 34:6. David's blessing on Jabesh calls down on them the same faithful love they had shown to their dead king.

Mashach, to anoint, the verb behind mashiach (anointed one) and so behind the title Messiah. David is anointed a second time, now publicly by his tribe. The repeated anointings (by Samuel, by Judah, by all Israel) trace how God's choice becomes recognized kingship.

Ach, brother. The word is used of blood brothers (Joab, Abishai, and Asahel) and of fellow Israelites. Abner's plea asks how long the troops will keep pursuing their brothers, and Joab repeats the word. The civil war is tragic precisely because the enemies are kin.

christ: David is anointed king over his own people while another claims the throne, and his kingdom grows gradually rather than all at once. The New Testament describes the kingdom of Christ in a similar way: Jesus is already the anointed king, yet his rule is still contested and grows like a seed until the day it fills the earth (Matthew 13:31-33). This is a pattern, not a prediction. David's reaching out to Jabesh, Saul's loyalists, with blessing rather than threat also anticipates the way the son of David invites former opponents into his kingdom. Hebron, where David's reign begins, is the city of Abraham, a reminder that the Davidic promise grows from God's older promise to Abraham, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:16).

hard.q: Why does David's rise involve so much killing among Israelites?
hard.a: The text does not hide the cost. The contest at Gibeon kills twenty-four young men for nothing, the battle kills hundreds, and Asahel's death starts a feud. The narrator presents this as tragedy, not triumph, and the chapter's most memorable speech is Abner's lament over brothers killing brothers. It is also notable that David himself is not shown ordering the battle; the commanders drive the violence, a pattern that will continue with Joab. Some readers see the chapter as an honest record of how kingdoms were actually formed in the ancient world, including God's chosen one; others emphasize that Scripture describes such violence to expose it, not to approve it. Either way the book does not suggest that God's purpose for David required these deaths, and it keeps the question open for the reader to feel.

questions: David asked God where to go even when the path to the throne seemed obvious. What decisions do you make without asking because the answer seems clear?
David honored the loyalty of people who had been on Saul's side. How do you treat those who were loyal to someone you opposed?
Abner asked whether the sword must devour forever. Where have you seen a conflict continue long after anyone remembered why it began, and what could end it?
